title: The 2026 Guide: x1 vs Claude Code (10 Key Differences)
summary: The world’s most powerful AI app studio. Build real iPhone apps one step at a time.
body_text: TL;DR x1 is an AI app studio that guides non-technical founders from a plain-English idea through planning, design, build, and App Store submission for native iPhone apps. Claude Code is a powerful agentic coding tool built for developers who already know how to manage repos, terminals, and Xcode. If your goal is a guided path to a real App Store launch, x1 is the better fit. If you are a developer who wants an AI agent inside your codebase, Claude Code is hard to beat. They are not the same category of tool, and comparing them on “which AI is smarter” misses the point entirely. The Real Question Behind x1 vs Claude Code Both x1 and Claude Code use AI to help build software. But they solve fundamentally different problems. x1 is an AI app studio for building and launching native iPhone apps. Claude Code is an agentic coding tool that runs in your terminal and can read files, edit code, run builds, manage Git, and automate development tasks across any language. The right choice depends on one thing: whether you need a guided app workflow or a coding agent. That distinction shapes everything, from who should use each tool, to what “done” looks like, to how much the total journey actually costs. This comparison is not abstract. Practitioners on Reddit, Medium, and LinkedIn have spent real time building iOS apps with Claude Code, and their experiences reveal patterns that matter for anyone deciding between these two paths. What follows are 10 concrete differences, grounded in actual user reports and product realities, to help you make the right call. Try x1 with free credits before committing to a full build. At-a-Glance Comparison Table Dimension x1 Claude Code Category AI app studio Agentic coding tool Best for Non-technical founders shipping native iOS apps Developers working in repos, terminals, and IDEs Output focus Native iPhone apps (Swift + Xcode) Any codebase or language, including iOS if configured Workflow coverage Plan, design, build, launch, iterate Explore, plan, edit, test, refactor, automate Technical skill required Lower; guided plain-English workflow Higher; assumes repo, toolchain, and debugging comfort Starting price $99/month (Builder); ~100 free credits available $20/month (Pro); Max from $100/month App Store support Built-in screenshots, listing, submission support Manual unless user builds their own workflow Biggest limitation iOS-only; younger product with less public proof Not a product studio; requires supervision and launch work Now, the full breakdown. 1. x1 Is an App Studio; Claude Code Is a Coding Agent This is the most important difference. Everything else flows from it. x1 is built to guide someone from an app idea to a finished, launchable iPhone app. It structures the process into five stages: Plan (map screens and features), Design (shape brand, layouts, and flow), Build (generate the native app screen by screen), Launch (create App Store assets and submit), and Iterate (refine post-build). For a closer look at how x1 works , the workflow moves in a deliberate sequence rather than relying on a single prompt window. Claude Code is a different animal. According to its official documentation, it operates as an agentic assistant inside the terminal. It reads repositories, edits files, searches codebases, runs shell commands, executes tests, manages Git, and works through an agentic loop of gathering context, taking action, verifying results, and repeating. It supports CLI, IDE, CI/CD, and more . A simple way to think about it: x1 is closer to a product team in a box. Claude Code is closer to a very capable AI developer inside your terminal. If you do not know what a terminal is, that distinction already tells you which tool fits. 2. x1 Is Built for Native iOS; Claude Code Is Language-Agnostic x1 focuses narrowly on native iPhone apps in Swift and Xcode. That narrow focus is the point. If iOS is the primary business wedge, and you want a native app rather than a cross-platform workaround, x1 is purpose-built for that path. Claude Code works across codebases and languages. It can support Swift and iOS projects, especially now that Apple’s Xcode 26.3 introduced agentic coding support with Claude Agent directly inside Xcode . That is a genuine improvement for developers building Apple-platform apps. But “can work on iOS” and “is designed for iOS” are not the same thing. Claude Code is better if the project spans backend, web, scripts, infrastructure, and multiple languages. x1 is better if native iOS is the whole job. If you are evaluating what an AI app studio actually is , the category distinction matters more than any feature list. 3. x1 Guides Planning Before Code; Claude Code Needs You to Bring the Plan Planning quality is one of the biggest determinants of AI app quality. A 2026 study on architecture descriptors for AI coding agents found that providing structured architecture context reduced navigation steps by 33 to 44 percent in code localization tasks and correlated with a 52% reduction in agent behavioral variance. The lesson is straightforward: the more the system knows about architecture, screens, and intent before it starts editing files, the less random the build becomes. x1’s Plan stage maps screens, features, flows, user actions, payment states, and return states before a single line of code is generated. This reduces “one-shot prompt” fragility, which is a well-documented problem with AI app builders that try to generate everything from a single description. Claude Code can help write specs and architecture, but the user must drive that process. Claude’s docs mention project-level CLAUDE.md files as a way to store conventions and context. That is useful for developers who know what to put there. It is less useful for someone who does not know what screens a subscription app needs, or what states each screen should handle. 4. x1 Includes Design and Screen Flow; Claude Code Mostly Edits Implementation Mobile apps are visual products. Code generation is not the same as product design. x1 provides a visual canvas for shaping brand, icon, colors, fonts, layouts, buttons, spacing, copy, and flow before the build step begins. This makes the design phase accessible to founders and designers who think visually, not in code. Claude Code can generate UI code, but visual quality depends on prompts, manual review, and the user’s ability to evaluate SwiftUI output. Xcode 26.3 improves this by letting agents visually verify Xcode Previews, which closes part of the feedback gap. Still, a practitioner on LinkedIn who compared Claude Code workflows across React Native and SwiftUI reported that React Native worked materially better for agentic coding because the agent could run builds, inspect the view hierarchy, take screenshots, and validate changes with less manual intervention. SwiftUI workflows required more manual Xcode rebuilds and validation. That feedback loop matters more than most people think. Claude Code can help build the UI. x1 is designed to help decide and shape the UI before code is generated. 5. x1 Handles the App Store Last Mile; Claude Code Leaves It to You This is where x1 vs Claude Code diverges most sharply for non-technical founders. x1’s Launch stage creates App Store screenshots, writes the App Store listing, and supports sending the app for review, all inside the same workflow. For more detail, see the full App Store submission workflow . Claude Code can help write scripts, draft metadata if prompted, and automate parts of a developer workflow. But the following tasks remain the builder’s responsibility when using Claude Code alone: Apple Developer Program enrollment ($99/year) Bundle ID, certificates, and provisioning profiles App Store Connect setup Screenshots and preview assets App title, subtitle, description, and keywords Privacy nutrition labels (required for all new apps and updates ) Privacy policy URL Subscription and paywall disclosures (Apple requires clear subscription information before purchase ) Test account and review notes App Review rejection handling x1’s advantage is not that Claude Code cannot help with these tasks. It is that x1 makes them part of the product workflow instead of a separate launch project. The App Store launch checklist covers what this process actually requires in practice. 6. Claude Code Is Cheaper to Start, but Not Always Cheaper to Finish On sticker price, Claude Code wins. Claude Pro costs $20/month (or $17/month billed annually at $200 upfront). Claude Max starts at $100/month with 5x or 20x more usage than Pro. Claude Code is included in all paid plans , though usage limits are shared across Claude web, desktop, mobile, and Claude Code. x1 pricing starts at $99/month for the Builder tier, $199/month for Pro, and $299/month for Max. Annual billing drops those to $66, $133, and $200 per month respectively. Around 100 free credits are available to try the product or build one feature. But subscription price is not the whole story. For a non-technical founder using Claude Code to build an iOS app, the hidden costs add up: Apple Developer Program: $99/year Developer time (or hired help) for Xcode setup, Git, signing, testing, and App Store Connect Potential Max subscription or API credits for heavy coding sessions Third-party tools for screenshots, ASO, privacy policies, analytics, and crash reporting Debugging time when AI output is “almost right” That last point is backed by data. Stack Overflow’s 2025 Developer Survey found that 66% of developers cite AI answers that are “almost right, but not quite” as their biggest AI frustration, and 45% say debugging AI-generated code takes more time than expected. If you only compare monthly subscriptions, Claude Code looks cheaper. If you compare the total cost of getting a non-technical founder to an App Store-ready native iOS app, x1 may be the more predictable path. For a deeper breakdown of total app costs, the app cost calculator walks through what most people miss. See x1 pricing and plan details . 7. Claude Code Gives More Control; x1 Gives More Constraints This is not a flaw in either tool. It is a design philosophy difference. Claude Code gives developers open-ended power. It works across any repo, lets you inspect and edit everything, supports terminal, IDE, CI/CD, MCP, hooks, plugins, subagents, and scheduled tasks. If you know what you are doing, the ceiling is very high. x1’s structured stages constrain choices in a way that helps beginners ship. The system asks questions at each step, maps decisions to screens, and moves through build in a deliberate order. This is less flexible than Claude Code, but it means users who do not know what to ask next still make progress. x1’s constraints help beginners ship. Claude Code’s openness helps developers customize. Both are valid. The question is which matches your skill set and timeline. 8. Claude Code Has More Public User Discussion; x1 Has Clearer Guided Positioning Honesty matters here. Claude Code has a large visible community footprint. Reddit threads, Medium posts, and LinkedIn discussions contain detailed, nuanced iOS and Swift feedback. x1, as a younger product, has less independent public review data. What Claude Code users say is revealing, though. A practitioner on Medium who stress-tested Claude Code by building a full iOS finance app reported that Claude Opus was excellent for ground-up architecture and complex problem-solving. But as the codebase grew, context size expanded, sessions shortened, and quota limits disrupted flow state . The recommendation was to use Opus strategically for architecture, then switch models for sustained implementation. Practitioners on Reddit in the r/swift community report similar patterns. One poster praised Claude Code for understanding broader context and coding style with less friction, but expressed frustration about limit changes despite paying $200/month. A commenter noted that Claude tends to produce “nicer code” and better organization, while other agents may allow more work before hitting limits. A LinkedIn practitioner who spent three months building a macOS app with Claude Code shared a pointed observation: roughly 50% of Claude’s code-review findings were false positives, and many corrections were about Apple ecosystem conventions rather than Swift syntax. The practitioner cited outdated patterns like suggesting ObservableObject and @StateObject instead of newer @Observable patterns in modern SwiftUI. The summary was blunt: “Claude knows Swift. It doesn’t know Apple.” x1’s case rests on a narrower promise: guided native iOS creation from idea to App Store. It has less chatter because it is a more focused product, not a general-purpose developer tool. Buyers should expect less public third-party validation than Claude Code, but a clearer workflow match for non-technical iOS app creation. 9. Mobile Agent Benchmarks Are Still Humbling for All AI Tools Before overcommitting to any AI tool for iOS, the research is worth knowing. SWE-Bench Mobile, a 2026 benchmark built from realistic iOS development tasks with PRDs, Figma designs, a mixed Swift/Objective-C codebase, and comprehensive tests, found that even the best agent-model configuration achieved only a 12% task success rate . The study also found that agent design matters as much as model capability, with up to a 6x performance gap using the same model across different agents. A separate study of 2,901 AI-authored pull requests across Android and iOS open-source repos found that iOS had a lower acceptance rate than Android : 63.7% vs 71.0%. The authors suggest iOS’s stricter design guidelines and development environment complexity contribute to the gap. The takeaway is not that AI cannot help build iOS apps. It clearly can. The takeaway is that the workflow surrounding the model, the constraints, the verification steps, the launch operations, matters as much as model intelligence. A focused iOS app studio can create value beyond raw model access because mobile app work requires requirements, visual design, architecture, testing, and launch operations, not just code generation. The future is not “pick the smartest model.” The future is “pick the workflow that gives the model the right context, constraints, verification, and launch path.” 10. Final Verdict: Choose Based on Your Role, Not the AI Here is the direct recommendation for x1 vs Claude Code. Pick x1 if you are: A non-technical founder with an iPhone app idea A solo founder who wants to ship iOS first A designer who wants control over screens and flow without becoming an iOS engineer A creator launching a companion app A small team validating a native iOS MVP Someone who wants App Store screenshots, listing, and submission support in one workflow Pick Claude Code if you are: An experienced developer comfortable with terminal, Git, and Xcode A technical founder with an existing repository An iOS developer who knows SwiftUI, testing, and App Store Connect A team building across backend, web, mobile, and infrastructure Someone who wants a coding agent, not a guided app studio Pick both if: A technical founder wants x1 for structured iOS product creation and Claude Code for advanced code review, backend work, or custom refactors An agency wants a guided iOS build workflow but uses Claude Code for internal engineering tasks The clearest way to frame x1 vs Claude Code: Claude Code is where developers go to work on code. x1 is where iOS-first founders go to turn an app idea into a launchable product. If your goal is “help me code,” choose Claude Code. If your goal is “help me turn my iPhone app idea into something I can submit to the App Store,” choose x1 . Frequently Asked Questions Is x1 better than Claude Code? x1 is better if you want a guided native iOS app workflow from idea to App Store. Claude Code is better if you are already a developer and want an AI agent inside your repo. They solve different problems, so the “better” answer depends entirely on whether you can code and whether you want to manage the full build and launch process yourself. Can Claude Code build an iPhone app? Yes. Claude Code can help build iPhone apps, especially with Xcode 26.3’s agentic coding support that lets agents like Claude work directly inside the Apple development environment. But it still requires technical supervision, Xcode and App Store knowledge, and manual launch work for screenshots, metadata, privacy labels, and submission. It is a coding agent, not a launch workflow. Which is cheaper, x1 or Claude Code? Claude Code is cheaper to start. Claude Pro costs $20/month, and Max starts at $100/month. x1 starts at $99/month with about 100 free credits to try. But the real comparison is not subscription price alone. For non-technical founders, the total cost of reaching a finished, App Store-ready native iOS app with Claude Code includes developer time, debugging, Apple Developer Program fees, third-party tools, and launch asset creation. x1 bundles more of that work into one workflow. Do I need to know how to code to use Claude Code? Practically, yes, if you want to use it for a real iOS app. Claude Code can generate and edit code, but you still need to understand build errors, repository state, testing, and whether the generated Swift and iOS code is correct. Practitioners on Reddit report that the Xcode route can overwhelm non-coders with simulator issues, provisioning confusion, and uncertainty about whether problems come from the AI’s code, Xcode, or the development environment itself. Does x1 replace Xcode? x1 guides users through planning, design, build, and launch for native iPhone apps from a web-based workflow. It is not positioned as a general-purpose Xcode replacement for professional iOS engineers. It is an AI app studio for people who want to build and launch native iOS apps without managing the full Apple developer toolchain themselves. For senior developers who want low-level Xcode control, Claude Code or direct development is a better fit. Can I use both x1 and Claude Code? Yes. A technical user could use x1 for the structured iOS app workflow and Claude Code for advanced engineering tasks, code review, backend scripts, or custom refactors. Non-technical users should not assume Claude Code is necessary unless they have someone available who can supervise code quality and handle developer tooling. What does x1 cost compared to hiring a developer? x1’s Builder plan starts at $99/month, or $66/month with yearly billing. Compared to hiring a freelance iOS developer (typically $5,000 to $25,000+ for a basic app), x1 is significantly less expensive for founders validating an MVP. The tradeoff is that x1 is iOS-only and does not offer the same flexibility as a custom engineering team. For a broader breakdown, the app builder selection checklist covers what to evaluate before choosing any approach. Is Claude Code good for SwiftUI? Claude Code can write competent SwiftUI code, and multiple practitioners praise its ability to produce clean, well-organized Swift. However, a LinkedIn practitioner who spent three months building with Claude Code found that it sometimes suggests outdated SwiftUI patterns and that Apple-platform correctness goes beyond Swift syntax. It includes modern lifecycle behavior, App Review expectations, privacy requirements, StoreKit integration, and Xcode project configuration. Claude Code is strong at writing code. Knowing whether that code follows current Apple conventions still requires human judgment.

title: Hillman to Acquire Kanebridge, Establishes Industrial Master Distribution Presence in U.S.
summary: Strategic Acquisition of Fastener Distributor Advances Hillman's Presence in Untapped Industrial Market  Increases Industrial Total…...
body_text: Hillman to Acquire Kanebridge, Establishes Industrial Master Distribution Presence in U.S. August 03, 2026 4:25pm EDT Download as PDF Strategic Acquisition of Fastener Distributor Advances Hillman's Presence in Untapped Industrial Market Increases Industrial Total Addressable Market to $3 Billion while Diversifying Customer and End-Market Exposure Unique Digital and Operational Platform Primed for Future Growth Opportunities CINCINNATI, Aug. 03, 2026 (GLOBE NEWSWIRE) -- Hillman Solutions Corp. (Nasdaq: HLMN) (the "Company", “Hillman Group”, or "Hillman"), a leading provider of hardware products and merchandising solutions, has entered into a definitive agreement to acquire Kanebridge Corporation ("Kanebridge"), a leading master distributor of industrial fasteners for a purchase price of $315 million, subject to customary adjustments for cash, indebtedness, working capital and transaction expenses. Kanebridge supplies more than 44,000 commercial and military-grade fastener SKUs to distributors throughout the U.S. and Canada from its warehouses in Illinois and California, selling exclusively to distributors in commercial and industrial channels. Kanebridge prides itself on maintaining industry-leading fill rates, its proprietary digital ordering platform, FasNet™, which enables same-day shipping, and its long-standing relationships with industrial and specialty distributors. These capabilities have made Kanebridge a critical partner for its customers for over 50 years. Consistent with Hillman's disciplined acquisition framework, the transaction is expected to be accretive to Hillman's margins and earnings. Hillman anticipates cost synergies from Hillman’s sourcing and distribution expertise, sales synergies coming from cross-selling opportunities, and material tax benefits from the transaction. Jon Michael Adinolfi, President and Chief Executive Officer of Hillman, commented: "Kanebridge gives us an immediate and credible foothold in the industrial channel, which we've identified as one of our biggest growth opportunities. Their master distributor model, capabilities-driven platform, and long-standing distributor relationships make it a great fit for us. This acquisition follows the same disciplined, accretive approach to M&A that has built Hillman over the past 60 years, and we're looking forward to welcoming the Kanebridge team to Hillman." Following completion of the acquisition, Kanebridge will operate as part of Hillman's commercial & industrial business, led by Chris Martin, EVP, Commercial & Industrial. Martin added: “Like Hillman, Kanebridge has decades of expertise taking great care of customers, maintaining strong fill rates, and providing a long tail of specialty fastener SKUs. Kanebridge's focus on the U.S. industrial market complements Hillman's existing industrial presence in Canada, broadening our combined reach across North America. The Kanebridge platform makes a great addition to our Commercial & Industrial business.” The acquisition advances Hillman's Industrial growth strategy, outlined at its recent Investor Day . The acquisition expands Hillman’s addressable market opportunity in industrial by $1 billion, bringing the total TAM to $3 billion. Kanebridge's master distributor model will leverage Hillman's global "dual faucet" sourcing expertise and extensive breadth of SKUs. Kanebridge gives Hillman an immediate, scaled platform to serve long-tail, high-specification fastener requirements across industrial and specialty distribution channels, while creating new cross-sell opportunities across Hillman's existing C&I, Pro and DIY customer base. The transaction has been approved by the boards of directors of both companies and is subject to regulatory approval and customary closing conditions. The Company expects to fund the transaction with a combination of cash from the balance sheet, borrowings under its existing asset-based revolving credit facility, and an add-on to its existing First Lien Term Loan, which the Company intends to raise through the capital markets. Advisors Jefferies LLC is acting as financial advisor and Thompson Hine LLP is acting as legal counsel to Hillman. Piper Sandler is acting as financial advisor and Koley Jessen P.C., L.L.O. is acting as legal counsel to Kanebridge. About Hillman Solutions Corp. Founded in 1964 and headquartered in Cincinnati, Hillman is a leading provider of hardware and related products serving retail, pro distribution, and industrial customers. Over the last 60-plus years, Hillman has built a legacy of service and growth by forming strategic partnerships with North America's leading home improvement, hardware, and farm and fleet retailers. Hillman differentiates itself from the competition with its dedicated field sales team of 1,200+ associates, direct-to-store distribution capabilities, and world class global sourcing and supply chain expertise. The company offers an extensive product portfolio of more than 111,000 SKUs, including fasteners (power screws, nuts, bolts), hardware (builder's hardware, door hardware, rope & chain, accessories), project gear & supplies (gloves, work gear, paint & cleaning sundries), and key and engraving services (key duplication, auto keys, and engraving). Hillman is committed to delivering exceptional customer service, innovative products, and dependable solutions to its customers and regularly earns vendor of the year recognition from top customers. For more information on Hillman, visit www.hillman.com . About Kanebridge Corporation Kanebridge Corporation is a leading U.S. master distributor of commercial and military-grade fasteners, serving distributors nationwide for more than 50 years. With more than 44,000 SKUs available for same-day shipment from warehouses in Illinois and California, Kanebridge is known for its product depth, fill-rate reliability, and specification expertise across inch and metric fastener categories. body_text: 2026 Hyundai Elantra N Reviews, Pricing & Specs Write a review $35,300 to $39,450 Original MSRP 7 of 10 expert review -- avg user rating (0 reviews) Pros Engaging and powerful Impressive grip and steering Useful performance tech and snug seats Cons Front axle fails to prevent axle hop and torque steer Imprecise clutch Plastic-heavy interior 7 out of 10 expert review Look & feel 4/10 Technology 7/10 Performance 8/10 Safety 7/10 Form & function 9/10 Cost-effectiveness 7/10 Since its introduction, Hyundai's raucous tuner car has learned some manners and it's now more fun to drive. Six new small cars packing the hottest turbocharged engines and performance upgrades cost between $35,000 and $53,000. The Hyundai Elantra N, at the bottom of that price range, transforms an ordinary compact into a thrilling sports sedan with a high level of power and poise that can be safely extracted on a public road. As a noisy, lowered car with a thirst for high-test gas, the Elantra N appeals solely to enthusiasts who want a track-tuned model from the factory at an affordable price. Despite some obvious faults, the latest Elantra N has been much improved since its first model year (2022). Remarkably, it’s even better with an automatic transmission. Verdict: Serious performance at an enticing price. 4/10 Styling doesn’t change for 2026, meaning the Elantra N remains as polarizing as ever. A new nose for 2024 gave the Elantra N a sleeker, slipperier appearance (and improved airflow), but this sedan is still festooned with a comical amount of slashes, creases, and jagged edges that means the design will likely age rapidly. We praise Hyundai for being original but, were we invited to consult for the next-generation Elantra, would strongly advise the designers to tone things down. Still, this is a distinctive model meant for people who don't want to disappear in a boring car. All the sills, spoilers and window trim are gloss black, with red accents. The exhaust outlets are several inches wide. The forged wheels and the red brake calipers are the classiest bits. In dark colors, these extraneous lines disappear into the paint, although they're in plain sight in Hyundai's Performance Blue, and it's a perfectly proportioned small sedan. Aside from the Volkswagen Golf R, there isn't a competitor that looks polished or expensive, to be fair. They all come off cheap, even though the added vents and aero are there for a purpose. Inside, the Elantra N keeps every plastic surface from the base Elantra, including a passenger grab handle that's as hard as a broomstick. Hustle along, and the driver's knees knock against hollow, unforgiving plastic, and the dashboard is no better, as it creaks and groans in reaction to any imperfect road surface. Other performance cars in this class feel like they won't become instant rattle traps. Honda, Acura, Volkswagen, and Toyota do a superior job with construction, but competitors from those brands are significantly pricier. Buyers should take that into consideration when purchasing an Elantra N and ask if they're here for a good time or a long time. The interior design itself is elevated, with a canted center stack, two crisp displays, and plenty of analog controls. One-piece Alcantara front seats with glowing backrests, a leather-wrapped steering wheel with BMW-like drive buttons, and a hefty shifter are where the money was spent. But the competition matches the Elantra N with these specialty items while doing a notably better job with the rest of their cabins. 8/10 Hyundai has a factory team in the IMSA Michelin Pilot Challenge series, specifically in the TCR class with modified production sedans such as the Audi RS 3 and the Honda Civic Type R. The company has won the manufacturers' championship six times in a row with the Elantra N, which says a lot about its racing partner, Bryan Herta Autosport, and the engineers in South Korea responsible for the production car. The Elantra N is powered by a 2.0-liter turbocharged inline-four making 276 horsepower and 289 pound-feet of torque sent to the front wheels through a limited-slip differential and either a six-speed manual or eight-speed dual-clutch automatic transmission. A dropped and retuned suspension with three-way adaptive dampers, 14.2-inch front brake rotors, and forged 19-inch wheels on Michelin Pilot Sport 4 S tires ensure the driver always receives maximum feedback. Everything, from the steering to the chassis brace behind the rear seat to the programmable driving modes, is unique to the Elantra N. The first 2022 model we tested was savage, and not in an entirely endearing way. The vague clutch engagement, heavy turbo lag, brittle ride, and gunshot exhaust felt more like an aftermarket experiment than a factory effort. It was still loads of fun, but incomplete. Hyundai has since revised the steering, suspension, and remapped the electronics, plus the forged wheels drop 33 pounds of unsprung weight, which adds to the N's eagerness to turn in. We tested the automatic for this review. Sorry to the three-pedal fans out there, but Hyundai doesn't make a good manual transmission. Its performance-tuned dual-clutch—which is fitted only to this car—is a gem that smooths out the N's power delivery, reduces turbo lag to almost nothing, and makes the car easier to launch while calming the powertrain at high speeds. We did not experience jerkiness or clunking as some other reviewers have noted. The three shift maps—which can be programmed in two custom driving modes, accessed on the touchscreen or by tapping either of the blue buttons on the steering wheel—range from daily comfort to neck-snapping fun. Plus, the dual-clutch comes with launch control (and an adjustable rev limit) and an F1-style "push to pass" button on the steering wheel that immediately drops to the lowest possible gear and allows 10 extra horsepower for 20 seconds at a time. It's a brilliant way to rip by slow traffic without worrying about what driving mode you're currently using. Fuel economy is reasonable, at 20 mpg city, 27 mpg highway, and 23 mpg combined. There's still some axle hop and torque steer, even in the dry, that are non-existent in the best front-wheel drive (FWD) competitors. Hyundai's suspension arrangement, while great on the track, doesn't fully measure up to hard use on the road where surfaces can be in constant flux. The Elantra N lacks all-wheel drive (AWD) which the Subaru WRX, the Volkswagen Golf R, and the Toyota GR Corolla use as an absolute ace up the sleeve. This is not a car buyers will want to drive even moderately hard in the wet, let alone the snow. Steering and braking are exemplary, and the body movements are well-controlled and nicely damped. They are the parts of the Elantra N that feel the most expensive and always satisfy. While the exhaust is quieter under full throttle, it's just as loud at city speeds in low gears, which may signal the ultimate intention for this car. We enjoyed the overruns and pops in first and second gear, and the low thrum at idle is addictive, not annoying. In just a few years, this high-strung Hyundai has matured in all the best ways. 9/10 For a small car, the Elantra N has a lot of interior space, especially in the back seat where it has significantly more legroom than any of its competitors. Sightlines are excellent in all directions and the trunk swallows 14.2 cubic feet, which is more than many midsize sedans, but the chassis brace will block taller, longer items from entering the cabin with the seats folded. Analog controls for the climate and stereo, and shortcut buttons for all the major functions (and most importantly, the many driving modes) are extremely welcome. Four of these buttons can be reprogrammed to call up a dozen or more functions that you can preselect in the main touchscreen. Seat comfort is excellent, too, and while the bolsters are fixed, they hug a 32-inch waist just right, so Elantra N buyers should watch their diet. The Elantra N comes in one trim with nearly every convenience feature as standard except for power seats or a sunroof, and the latter is only paired with the automatic. Full LED exterior lighting, power heated mirrors, a proximity key, heated front seats, dual-zone climate control, a wireless charging pad, and four USB ports are all standard. Adaptive cruise control and heated rear seats are unavailable, though. 7/10 The Elantra N's shining tech feature is the N app, which displays real-time data on the current gear, throttle position, brake pedal pressure, horsepower, and much more. Built-in presets can optimize the car for specific racetracks across the U.S., while additional options allow the driver to set shift warning lights, launch control revs, the N Grin Shift (the "push to pass" fast-shifting function) and record acceleration and lateral Gs. It's especially easy to set up the two custom driving modes. Multiple tiles for each adjustment (throttle, steering, suspension, transmission, differential, exhaust) make the ramp-up from Normal to Sport+ easy to decipher. The dual 10.25-inch displays are crisp, especially the instrument panel which in N mode shifts to a single, central tachometer with readouts of the turbo pressure, oil temperature, and other vitals. The downside is the infotainment software, which is an older version than in many other Hyundai models. Small, unclear icons in the same color are difficult to view at a glance. Apple CarPlay and Android Auto are not wireless, and only the older USB-A port supports phone projection, not the USB-C port, which is for power only. Blind-spot monitors and surround-view camera systems are not here, either. But the setup menus are clear and make customizing the Elantra N's functions very easy. An eight-speaker Bose stereo, SiriusXM, and HD radio are standard, along with Wi-Fi and a digital phone key. Additional remote connectivity is available with the Bluelink+ app on a smartphone or smartwatch. 7/10 While the Elantra N is not separately rated in crash tests, it is identical to the Elantra and Elantra Hybrid models that have been tested in this generation, and the National Highway Traffic Safety Administration (NHTSA) rated the 2026 Elantra and Elantra Hybrid five stars overall. The Insurance Institute for Highway Safety (IIHS) tested the 2021 Elantra and applied those tests to the 2026 model, which received a Top Safety Pick award, including the best Good rating in three crash tests. There are no rear side airbags or front knee airbags, and only the front seats are equipped with seat belt pre-tensioners. The Elantra N isn’t available with every driver assist feature in Hyundai’s catalog, with the Highway Driving Assist system being one notable absence. The list is nonetheless comprehensive, including automatic emergency braking with pedestrian detection, front and rear parking sensors, lane-keep assist, a driver-attention monitor, blind spot monitors, high-beam assist, and a safe-exit warning for the rear doors. 7/10 The 2026 Hyundai Elantra N starts at $35,100 and comes in a single trim. Adding the automatic transmission costs $1,500 and Performance Blue, Ultimate Red, and Cyber Gray paints each add $500. With both options and the destination fee, our car was $38,345. Fully loaded, the Elantra N is $10,000 less than a loaded Toyota GR Corolla and more than $12,000 beneath the starting price of a Volkswagen Golf R. The Subaru WRX, however, represents the segment's best value and starts nearly $3,000 less than the Elantra N. All those competitors have AWD, which is a huge benefit that should not be overlooked. Hyundai's five-year, bumper-to-bumper warranty is two years longer than most of its competitors, and on a high-performance car with expensive hardware, that alone may be worth it. Ultimately, the Elantra N is very satisfying and would continue to be a great pick even if it were more expensive. title: Best power dialers in 2026: 6 tools compared
summary: We compared the best power dialers for sales teams. See which one fits your CRM, your budget, and the kind of dialing your reps actually do.
body_text: Article overview A power dialer automates outbound calling so reps stop copying, pasting, and dialing numbers by hand. The right choice depends on three things: your CRM, the type of dialer you need, and your budget. Real starting costs range from $45 per month for one user with Allo to $350 per month for five with Aloware, once seat minimums are included. Introduction You've set up the best lead generation pipeline possible. Signals, a research agent, enrichment. It all runs on autopilot. But your team still spends their days copying phone numbers, pasting them into a softphone, and calling prospects one by one. Every manual dial is a few seconds of friction. Multiply that across a day, and your reps lose hours to admin instead of conversations. That's exactly where a power dialer helps. A power dialer automates the mechanical part of outbound calling. Your reps talk more and type less. It contributes to accelerating your sales . In this guide, we explain what a power dialer is, how to pick the right one for your team, and share our favorites. What is a power dialer? A power dialer is software that automatically dials phone numbers from a list, one after another. The rep doesn't touch the keypad. As soon as one call ends, the system dials the next contact. The goal is simple. A power dialer removes the dead time between calls. Reps skip the manual dialing, the misdials, and the wait for voicemail beeps. Most power dialer software also logs each call into your CRM automatically. Call recordings, notes, and outcomes sync back without any copy-paste. Modern tools add AI on top: transcription, summaries, and next-step suggestions. A power dialer is usually part of a broader cloud phone system. That means it's hosted in the browser, needs no hardware, and works wherever your reps are. What are the different types of power dialers? "Power dialer" is often used as a catch-all term. In practice, there are several types, and each one fits a different calling style: Single-line power dialer. This is the classic power dialer. It dials one contact at a time, automatically, right after the previous call ends. The rep is always live for the conversation, so there's no awkward pause when the prospect picks up. This type works best for teams that value connection quality over raw volume. It’s also the most ethical kind of power dialer. Allo, Aircall, Aloware and Dialpad use this approach. Parallel (multi-line) dialer. A parallel dialer calls several numbers at the same time. When someone answers, it connects them to an available rep and drops the other lines. This type works best for high-volume prospecting into cold lists, where pickup rates are low. CloudTalk, JustCall, and CallHippo offer parallel dialing. Predictive dialer. A predictive dialer uses algorithms to dial ahead of agent availability. It predicts when a rep will be free and paces the calls to match. This type works best for large call centers with many agents dialing constantly. JustCall and dedicated contact-center platforms like Five9 (not covered in this article) offer predictive dialing. Preview dialer. A preview dialer shows the rep the contact's details before the call starts. The rep gets a moment to read the record, then triggers the dial. This type works best for complex or high-value sales, where preparation matters more than speed. Most power dialers include a contact preview. AI power dialer. An AI power dialer layers artificial intelligence onto any of the above. It transcribes calls, writes summaries, scores conversations, and sometimes runs an AI voice agent for the first touch. Allo, Dialpad, and Aloware lead here. A quick note on volume and compliance. Parallel and predictive dialers create the highest call volume, but they also carry more regulatory risk because of dropped or abandoned calls. We cover the legal side in the FAQ. Once you know which type you need, choosing a specific tool gets much easier. How to pick the right power dialer Three questions narrow the field fast: Start with your CRM . A power dialer that doesn't sync with your CRM will cost you the time it was supposed to save. Check for a native integration first, not just a Zapier connection. If you run HubSpot, look specifically for a HubSpot power dialer that pushes call recordings and transcripts back into the contact record. If you run Salesforce, confirm the dialer supports it. Some tools only power-dial from one CRM. Evaluate which kind of dialer you need . Match the dialer type to your motion. A small team calling warm, qualified leads is best served by a single-line power dialer. A team burning through large cold lists benefits from a parallel dialer. A large call center with constant dialing may need a predictive dialer. Don't pay for parallel dialing you won't use. Match it with your budget . Costs vary greatly, and two numbers matter. The first is the per-seat price of the plan that includes the power dialer, which runs from $45 to $110 per user per month in the tools below. The second is the seat minimum, which some vendors set at 3 to 10 licenses. Together they set your real starting cost. Annual billing usually saves 25 to 30 percent. With those three filters in mind, here are our six picks, ordered by real starting cost. Allo: best for small sales teams that want an affordable, AI-first dialer Allo overview Allo is an AI and mobile-first phone system built for small teams, SMBs, and salespeople. The product is designed around two ideas: AI included by default and the tool is agent-friendly, and pricing that stays simple. Every plan ships with AI features, and there are no per-feature add-ons. Allo holds a 4.7/5 on G2 across 200+ reviews. Allo's power dialer Allo includes a single-line power dialer. It dials your list one contact at a time, so the rep is always live when a prospect answers. There's no parallel dialer, and that's intentional. Allo optimizes for conversation quality, not raw volume. You can build your dialing queue in several ways. Import from a CRM, a CSV, or an API. You can even populate the queue through an LLM, thanks to Allo's MCP integration with tools like Claude and Codex. Reps can pause a dialing session at any time. The surrounding sales features are where Allo stands out for its price: Native CRM integrations sync call recordings, transcriptions, and contact updates automatically. The HubSpot integration is rated 5/5 on the HubSpot marketplace and 4.5/5 on the Pipedrive equivalent . Allo also includes call transcription and summaries, AI call tags, custom summary templates, an AI assistant that answers questions from your call history. An AI receptionist handles inbound calls in French, Spanish, or English. It remembers the previous discussions your prospects had with you and can even book appointments in your calendar. Allo pricing The power dialer is included in the Business plan which costs $45 per user per month ($32 billed yearly). The plan includes all integrations, a collaborative inbox, custom AI summary templates, AI call tags, the Allo MCP, and analytics. Unlike some other solutions included below, it has no seat minimum. There's a 7-day free trial and you can cancel anytime from the app. Who Allo works best for We're convinced Allo works best for small sales teams that use HubSpot, Salesforce, Pipedrive, or Attio and want deep, two-way CRM sync without paying enterprise prices. It fits teams that want AI included rather than sold as an add-on, and that value connection quality over dialing many leads at once. Teams that need parallel dialing or complex enterprise call flows should look further down this list. Allo keeps AI affordable for small teams. Dialpad also includes AI in every plan, but it targets Salesforce users and carries the highest per-seat price here. Dialpad: best for Salesforce teams that want the strongest built-in AI Dialpad overview Dialpad was founded in 2011 and serves SMBs through mid-market companies and runs its own AI model, developed in-house since 2018. It maintains separate products for general use (Connect), support, and sales (Sell). Dialpad holds a 4.4/5 on G2 across more than 4,000 reviews. Dialpad's power dialer Dialpad's power dialer lives inside Dialpad Sell. It imports contacts via CSV, API, or Salesforce, and Salesforce is the only supported CRM for the dialer. That's an important limitation if you run HubSpot or Pipedrive. The dialer itself is strong. Voicemail drop, real-time call monitoring with live sentiment and transcripts, and detailed calling rules (time zones, attempt limits, Do Not Contact) are all built in. Dialpad's AI is the differentiator, with live coaching, call scoring, and AI Playbooks that track rep adherence to methodologies like BANT or SPIN. There's no parallel dialer. Dialpad pricing Dialpad Sell is priced separately from Dialpad Connect. The power dialer is included in two plans: Advanced: $110 per user per month ($95 yearly). Adds local presence, voicemail drop, the Salesforce power dialer, and AI Live Coach. Premium: $170 per user per month ($150 yearly). Adds AI Scorecards, AI Playbooks, and ACD. There's a 14-day free trial and no minimum seat count. Who Dialpad works best for Dialpad works best for Salesforce-based sales teams that want the deepest built-in AI coaching and can justify a premium per-seat price. The AI is genuinely best in class and included by default. But the power dialer only works with Salesforce, there's no parallel dialing, and at $110 per user per month it's the most expensive option here on a per-seat basis. Teams on other CRMs should pick a different tool. Dialpad's dialer only works with Salesforce and stays single-line. JustCall supports more CRMs and adds parallel and predictive dialing. JustCall: best for teams that need parallel and predictive dialing JustCall overview JustCall is a phone system aimed at sales and support teams. It works in 70+ countries and integrates widely with CRMs. It carries a 4.3/5 on G2 across more than 2,300 reviews and a 3.8/5 on Trustpilot. Justcall’s rating on Truspilot JustCall's power dialer JustCall offers the widest range of dialer types on this list. It includes a power dialer, a parallel dialer with up to 10 simultaneous calls, and a predictive dialer that dials multiple numbers and connects reps only when a human answers. The feature set is built for serious outbound. It covers voicemail drop, local presence, territory controls with per-region calling windows, DNC (Do Not Contact) compliance, and live call monitoring. An outbound AI voice agent can qualify leads before a rep picks up. JustCall integrates natively with HubSpot, Salesforce, Pipedrive, Attio, Salesloft, and more. It scores 4/5 on both the HubSpot and Pipedrive marketplaces. JustCall pricing The power dialer is included in two plans: Pro: $69 per user per month ($49 yearly), minimum 2 licenses. Includes the power dialer, bulk SMS, and Salesforce integration. Pro Plus: $109 per user per month ($89 yearly). Adds real-time agent assist, sentiment analysis, and call scoring. Real starting cost: $138 per month on monthly billing (2 seats at $69), or $98 per month billed yearly (2 seats at $49), which is $1,176 per year. Note that most AI features sit behind add-ons: "AI Review Assist" at $9 per user per month, and the AI Voice Agent at $99 per month for 100 minutes. There's a 14-day free trial. Who JustCall works best for JustCall works best for outbound teams that want power, parallel, and predictive dialing under one roof, plus strong compliance controls. It's a natural fit for higher-volume prospecting where pickup rates are low. Keep in mind that the AI layer is priced separately, so the real monthly cost climbs once you add transcription and coaching. JustCall packs several dialer types into one plan. CloudTalk takes a narrower focus: international reach with local presence built in. CloudTalk: best for international outbound teams CloudTalk overview CloudTalk is a cloud phone system that serves sales and support teams, including call centers, and boasts 4,000 customers across 100 countries. Its standout strength is international reach: local numbers in 160+ countries. It holds a 4.4/5 on G2 across roughly 1,850 reviews. CloudTalk's power dialer CloudTalk offers a full-featured power dialer plus an optional parallel dialer. The power dialer imports contacts from a CSV or CRM, lets agents fill in surveys during calls, and includes voicemail drop and call scripts. A local presence feature automatically picks a caller ID in the prospect's area code to boost pickup rates. For higher volume, CloudTalk sells a parallel dialer as an add-on. It calls up to 10 lines at once, but it costs an extra $39 per user per month and is billed annually only. CloudTalk pricing The power dialer sits on the Expert plan ($69 per user per month, $49 yearly), which requires 3 licenses. Real starting cost: $207 per month on monthly billing (3 seats at $69), or $147 per month billed yearly (3 seats at $49), which is $1,764 per year. The parallel dialer is an add-on on top of Expert. There's a 14-day free trial, no credit card required. Who CloudTalk works best for CloudTalk works best for outbound teams that call across many countries and want local presence built in. The 160+ country coverage and automatic local caller ID are hard to match. Just budget for the parallel dialer add-on if you need multi-line dialing, and note the 3-seat minimum on the plan that includes the power dialer. CloudTalk sells parallel dialing as an add-on. Aircall keeps outbound lighter and leans instead on its brand and its integration catalog. Aircall: best for teams that want a proven brand with deep CRM integrations Aircall overview Aircall targets medium-sized and large companies, and it's one of the most recognized names in the category. It holds a 4.4/5 on G2 across roughly 1,600 reviews. Aircall's power dialer Aircall includes a single-line power dialer aimed at teams that cold-call responsibly. It's intentionally simpler than a dedicated outbound tool. There's no parallel dialer, which Aircall has stated is a deliberate choice, and no local presence option. Screenshot of a blog article on Aircall’s website that explains why they don’t offer a parallel dialer What it does well is the workflow around the call. Voicemail drop lets reps leave a pre-recorded message with one click. The dialer also pulls CRM context before each call. Aircall's real strength is its integration ecosystem, with deep native connections to HubSpot, Salesforce, Pipedrive, Zoho, Intercom, and more. Aircall pricing The power dialer is included in the Professional plan: $70 per user per month ($50 yearly). Includes voicemail drop, and advanced analytics. 3 licenses minimum. Real starting cost: $210 per month on monthly billing (3 seats at $70), or $150 per month billed yearly (3 seats at $50), which is $1,800 per year. AI features are an add-on (AI Assist from $9 per user per month). There's a 7-day free trial. Who Aircall works best for Aircall works best for teams that want a trusted, plug-and-play brand with a very large integration catalog, and whose outbound motion is light rather than high-volume. Smaller teams should note the 3-seat minimum and that support skews toward larger accounts. Aircall keeps things simple. Aloware goes the other way, toward contact-center scale and volume. Aloware: best for contact centers and high-volume calling plus SMS Aloware overview Aloware began in 2018 as a call-tracking tool, pivoted into a modern dialer, and grew into a full contact center built for remote teams. It targets sales and support teams and contact centers. It's a smaller, more niche player than the big UCaaS names, with a 4.1/5 on G2 across more than 800 reviews. Aloware's power dialer Aloware is built around high-volume outbound for support teams. Its AI-powered dialer lets a single agent handle multiple calls, and the platform layers in automation, texting, and CRM syncing. Reps can "park" calls while they look up information, and support-style inbox tabs (open, pending, closed) help teams track conversations. The AI features, including transcriptions, summaries, sentiment analysis, and talk-to-listen ratios, are included in all plans, with more advanced coaching and monitoring on the top tier. HubSpot integration is a particular strength, including workflow and list sync. Aloware pricing The power dialer is available in two plans: uPro + AI: $70 per user per month ($60 annually), minimum 5 users. Adds the AI-powered dialer, HubSpot workflow integration, call coaching, and full API access. xPro + AI: $100 per user per month ($85 annually), minimum 5 users. Adds Salesforce integration and unlimited AI voice analytics. Real starting cost: $350 per month (5 seats at $70). There's a 7-day free trial, no credit card required. Cancellation runs through an online form 30 days before renewal. Who Aloware works best for Aloware works best for growing contact centers and high-volume sales teams on HubSpot that combine heavy calling with texting automation. The AI-powered dialer and included AI analytics suit teams making hundreds of touches a day. The seat minimums of 5 to 10 users make it a poor fit for very small teams. Conclusion The best power dialer is the one that matches your CRM, your dialing style, and your budget. There's no single winner for every team. For small, AI-first sales teams that want deep CRM sync at a fair price, Allo is our top pick, with a real starting cost of $45 per month for one user. For Salesforce teams that want the strongest built-in AI, choose Dialpad, from $110 per month for one user. For teams that need power, parallel, and predictive dialing in one tool, choose JustCall, from $138 per month for two seats. For international outbound with local presence built in, choose CloudTalk, from $207 per month for three seats. For a proven brand with a huge integration catalog and a light outbound motion, choose Aircall, from $210 per month for three seats. For high-volume contact centers that combine calling and texting on HubSpot, choose Aloware, from $350 per month for five seats. Start with your CRM, confirm the dialer type you actually need, and use the free trials before you commit. FAQ What is a power dialer? A power dialer is software that automatically dials phone numbers from a list, one after another, so reps don't dial manually. As soon as one call ends, it dials the next contact. Most power dialers also log calls to your CRM and add AI features like transcription and summaries. It's usually part of a cloud (hosted) phone system, so it needs no hardware. Why use a power dialer? A power dialer removes the dead time between calls. Reps stop copying, pasting, and misdialing numbers, so they spend more time talking to prospects. It also standardizes follow-up, because calls, recordings, and notes sync to the CRM automatically. The result is more conversations per hour and cleaner data. Is it legal to use a power dialer? In most cases, yes, but it depends on how you dial and where. In the US, outbound calling is governed by the TCPA and by federal and state Do Not Call rules. Single-line power dialers, where a rep is live for each call, generally carry lower regulatory risk than predictive or parallel dialers, which can create abandoned calls. To stay compliant, honor Do Not Contact lists, respect calling-hour windows, and get consent where required. This is general information, not legal advice, so check the rules for your region and industry. Is there a free power dialer? Fully free power dialers are rare, but most tools offer a free trial. Allo, Aircall, and Aloware run 7-day trials, and CloudTalk and JustCall run 14-day trials. A few CRMs also bundle a basic dialer. How much is a power dialer? It depends on the per-seat price of the plan that includes the dialer and on the seat minimum. The real starting cost is the two multiplied together. title: In Conversation With Jan Robert Leegte
summary: Jan Robert Leegte on making art about software, not with it, and his solo presentation of JPEG, Sightings, and Orbits at Art Basel Zero 10.
body_text: Jan Robert Leegte has been making art on and about the internet since 1997, placing him among the pioneers of what became known as net art. Where others used the internet as a delivery mechanism, Leegte made the internet's own systems, its scrollbars, selection marquees, raw code, and compression algorithms, the subject and material of his practice. His work has been exhibited at the Centre Pompidou, the Whitechapel Gallery, the Stedelijk Museum Amsterdam, and the Van Gogh Museum, and has been acquired by private and institutional collections worldwide. He is represented by Upstream Gallery in Amsterdam and Office Impart in Berlin. In this conversation, Leegte speaks with OpenSea about his solo presentation at Art Basel Zero 10, where he brought together three bodies of work: JPEG , Sightings , and Orbits , united by an investigation into compression as one of the hidden infrastructures of digital image culture. He discusses how compression moves across artistic traditions, from abstract painting to snapshot photography to early animation, what it means to hold a procedural work on the blockchain, and why, nearly 30 years into his practice, the networked computer remains his central subject. Art Basel booth. Image courtesy of artist. OpenSea: You've been making art on the internet since 1997, and your work has been shown at the Centre Pompidou, the Whitechapel Gallery, and the Van Gogh Museum. But Art Basel is a different kind of context. What did it mean to bring this work to Zero 10, and how did you think about presenting it in a space designed for the traditional art market? Jan Robert Leegte: Over the years I’ve done quite a lot of solo presentations at galleries and art fairs. Although the context is commercial, I’ve been lucky to work with galleries [Upstream Gallery and Office Impart] that really support experimentation. So I’ve always stretched the context to make them into exhibitions. A coherent statement with a diversity of works. For Zero 10 I sent a proposal in the same manner. Zero 10 is also special, as it stimulates this way of presenting, being between an art fair and a curated show. OpenSea: Zero 10 was curated around the theme "The Condition." How did you read that framing in relation to your own work, and did it shape how you put the presentation together? Jan Robert Leegte: The proposal preceded the theme, but it aligned precisely. My work very much looks at the networked computer as a condition, and takes that as its starting point. I don’t use software to make art, I make art about software. In my early years I saw that the internet was an extension of sculpture, and I wanted to take that field as my subject and material. What does it mean to make art on the internet, not as content delivered through it, but as a reflection of it? The works I showed are investigations on the materiality of the networked computer. OpenSea: JPEG, Sightings, and Orbits are three distinct bodies of work, but at Art Basel you brought them together around a shared investigation into compression. What connects them for you, and how did you land on compression as the organizing idea? Jan Robert Leegte: I’ve dived into all kinds of aspects of the internet to work with, and compression is one of those lineages. My works always are tethered to art history as a way to find my way back and to take people with me on my journey into this new field of art. JPEG is rooted in abstract painting. I had two new projects using compression that veered into very different disciplines, photography and animation. I thought it would be an interesting unfolding: how a single material opens onto such different artistic traditions. OpenSea: The JPEG series makes visible something that's normally meant to be invisible: the algorithm running underneath every image on the internet. What does it look like to generate an image from compression alone, with no underlying photograph, and what drew you to that as a problem? Jan Robert Leegte: I’d worked with live compression before, with the series Compressed Landscapes. These net art pieces continuously fetch landscape images from the net and compress them in the browser in a contemporary interpretation of Impressionism, where the outside is the internet, and the artist the algorithm. The compression codec is how the internet sees images, and is amplified to show this “impression”. JPEG was born from the blockchain. As I couldn’t use images and only a little code, I was inspired to make a more radical work and use code and codec only to create a work. In the ethos of the abstract expressionists, this was not a JPEG depicting an image. The JPEG was the image itself. OpenSea: You've written about Orbits as a world that exists only in the instant it is compressed, orbiting only because someone is watching, and about that threshold where the mind starts filling in continuity between frames. How much of the work is actually happening in the viewer's head? Jan Robert Leegte: The idea of discrete frames becoming continuous, happening in your head, is 200 years old and the base of animation and cinema, in fact all motion on your computer screen: interface transitions, games, or YouTube. But I deliberately chose the threshold of 12 frames per second as it resembled the rawness of becoming an image like the code-generated compression spaces. The work is all code, but creates this strange place, through its crudeness. It’s like it just falls into existence out of abstraction. Sighting No 10 by Jan Robert Leegte OpenSea: Sightings is a new work that premiered at Basel. What can you tell us about where it came from, and what is it doing that JPEG and Orbits aren't? Jan Robert Leegte: Sightings was born from experimenting with the JPEG engine I had programmed. I wanted to see what else I could create and added random specks and lines. When I looked back, instantly the work had shifted from the domain of abstract painting to snapshot photography. The compression artifacts stopped being painterly gestures, and flipped back to zoomed-in images. Narratives would pour out, what is this setting, where is this? UFOs? Drones, missiles, satellites, planes, spacecraft? By combining the three series, coded compression moved from abstract painting through amateur photography to early film experimentation. OpenSea: These works exist as code and as large physical objects at the same time: dye sublimation on aluminium, prints, generative collections. You've talked before about how taking work out of the computer helps you understand it differently. What does a 200 x 300 cm physical print of a JPEG compression algorithm show you that the screen version doesn't? Jan Robert Leegte: By having the pigment baked onto metal, which you can actually touch, on a scale that encapsulates your whole body, the result becomes deeply visceral. It echoes the tradition of Rothko and Newman, where painting becomes the condition of the space and your body. Here I try to take a layer from software and present it in that tradition. It is a way of experiencing a digital entity of a fundamental level many have never experienced before. It teaches you not to take these digital materials for granted, but let them be the center of presence. OpenSea: Compression has been the invisible infrastructure of the image-based internet since the early nineties, and now it's also the substrate underneath AI-generated images. Do you see your work as being in conversation with that, and where does the investigation go from here? Jan Robert Leegte: Sightings especially has an interesting dialogue with AI-generated images as they both are code-generated images, created artificially by computer algorithms. But Sightings does something else, it doesn’t use any source material whatsoever. It is purely generative, letting the compression be the guide in letting the image arise in your head. I kind of like how I presented this body of work now, at the dawn of AI, closing a chapter of decades of procedural image generation and showing how ongoing development in computation builds on earlier structures, in this case this 1992 codec. I committed myself to explore what the networked computer means for art in 1997. That commitment hasn't changed. As the network keeps unfolding, I will follow that call. Orbit 68 by Jan Robert Leegte OpenSea: OpenSea acquired a piece from Orbits for its Flagship Collection, which holds work chosen for its long-term cultural significance. You describe Orbits as a world "orbiting only because we are watching." What does it mean to you for a work like that to be collected and held for the long term? Jan Robert Leegte: This connects to a long tradition in conceptual and process art. A Sol LeWitt wall drawing is not collected as a fixed object. You hold the instruction and the right to let the work be realised again. The value sits in the concept and its conditions, not in a frozen artefact. Orbits belong to that lineage. Each token is a procedural work, not a static image, so what is collected is the process itself, still arising when watched. Blockchain is the perfect medium to hold this. It is built to keep code alive and executable, far into the future. The medium matches the work. A piece about generation is held by a system designed to keep generating. title: Scaling a team with purpose: Why I joined Cinder
body_text: On my first day as Cinder's founding recruiter, the founders walked me through how they got started in this work. They met working on the trust and safety team at Facebook, which made complete sense to me. Anyone who's spent five minutes on Facebook knows there's a tremendous amount of bad stuff happening on the platform at any given moment, and of course a company that size has a massive team dedicated to keeping users safe from it. That part of the story tracked. “Wait, they need trust and safety?!” Where my mind really exploded was when they started talking about all the OTHER platforms that needed trust and safety resources: E-commerce marketplaces, video game companies, online fitness communities, open source platforms. Whole categories of products I've used for years without ever once thinking about the fact that they have trust and safety problems, too. I'd genuinely never connected those dots, in part because I've personally never experienced any harm on any of those apps, which made it harder for me to imagine other people having a negative experience. But of course they were. Of course they are. As co-founder Phil Brennan can attest, my reaction, more than once and out loud, was something like: "Wait, they need Cinder?" I felt my brain rewiring. If your platform lets users upload anything , or talk to each other, or transact in any way at all, someone has to defend the people using it from the people trying to exploit it. Bullying, scams, NCII, child predators, AI models being manipulated into telling a kid how to hurt themselves. Every app I'd ever opened on my phone suddenly had a hidden layer I'd never thought about, and behind that layer were teams of people doing some of the hardest and most underappreciated work on the internet. I hadn't really known any of this before I joined. Speed, scrappiness, and shaping culture The introduction came through a LinkedIn DM, right as I was wrapping up maternity leave with my second daughter. Tina Wu, a former coworker of mine, and one of Cinder’s earliest engineering hires, pinged me to say Cinder was looking for their first in-house recruiter, and my name had come up. I'd spoken to one of Cinder's cofounders a couple of years earlier, as a favor to Tina, back when the company was only about five people. It was the kind of early-stage conversation about which tools to invest in, how to think about agency support versus in-house, and what the first few hires should look like. At the time I hadn’t registered what Cinder did, so after chatting with Tina, I started digging in. The more I learned, the more things started lining up. I already knew four team members because we’d worked together at a previous startup, and they were all fantastic. Like them, I was coming from public safety software and figured the leap to trust and safety wouldn't be enormous. The stage of the company was one I knew well and genuinely love. This would be my third sub-30-person startup in the last decade, and there's something about this particular moment in a company's life that I find more energizing than almost anything else in this work: the scrappiness, the speed, the way every hire shapes the culture, the fact that you're convincing people to bet on something that didn't exist in their world a week ago. The shape of what Cinder needed was something I'd lived through before, and the more I sat with it the more I wanted to do it again with this team, and this mission. Early stage founding principles The one thing sitting in the back of my mind was whether I was actually ready to jump back into the intensity of this stage. I had a newborn and a toddler at home, and I'd be the only person owning recruiting end to end. I know how demanding building from this point feels, and I didn't want to romanticize it or pretend it would be easy. My final interview was a ninety-minute walk along the Williamsburg waterfront with Glen, Cinder's co-founder and CEO. Every challenge he described was one I'd been through before, and I had stories from my last two startups that resonated with him, too. The whole thing felt like catching up with someone I'd known for years, not a first-time meeting with a CEO. One of my non-negotiables when joining an early-stage company is that the founders have to be genuinely inspiring. When things get heavy, and they will, you need a leader with a clear vision and real energy to pull people through. I'd been lucky to have that at my last two startups, and walking back from that waterfront conversation, I knew Glen had it too. By the time the offer came, I was already totally bought in. My husband joked with me that he knew I’d accept from the first conversation I had. Every day since, I've felt strong conviction that this was the right move. Finding our why: The important reason we do this work. One extremely challenging part of this work is important to note. We talk about the worst things on the internet every single day. Articles about child predators, AI chatbots harming kids, NCII takedowns, the kind of content most people will never have to think about, let alone look at. Our customers are the trust and safety teams working to protect the internet from these abuses at scale, and our product is what makes it survivable for them. It's heavy, and I won't pretend otherwise. But it's also the first time in my career that the end-users we're ultimately protecting feel truly universal. Cinder is different. Everyone is on the internet, every single day. Almost everyone I know has, at some point, had a brush with harm on a platform: a scam, a harassing message, a piece of content they wish they hadn't seen. The mission is universally legible in a way I've never experienced before. The other reason I love being here as our founding recruiter is that I get to help shape who builds the next version of this company. I'm not just filling seats. I'm thinking about the team that twenty Cinder employees from now will look back on as the group that set the bar for everything that came after. Moving fast, making strong calls with imperfect information, convincing brilliant people to bet on a company they hadn't heard of a week ago, and, for the first time in my career, doing all of it with AI tools that didn't exist six months ago, is genuinely fun in a way that's hard to overstate. If you're reading this because you're considering Cinder, I want you to know what you're actually signing up for. The work is hard, the subject matter is heavy, and the pace is unforgiving. But you'll go home at night knowing exactly what you did and who it was for, which is rarer than it should be. That's why I joined.

title: XTI Aerospace announces executive leadership transition
summary: Scott Pomeroy has resigned as chairman and chief executive officer, the company said.
body_text: XTI Aerospace, Inc., an aerospace and advanced technology platform and parent company of Drone Nerds, LLC, a drone solutions platform serving commercial, enterprise and government customers, announced two leadership changes designed to streamline management and position the company to address the significant growth opportunities across the commercial, industrial and defense drone markets. Effective immediately, Scott Pomeroy has resigned as chairman and chief executive officer. The board of directors has appointed Jeremy Schneiderman as interim CEO, and elected Jonathan Ornstein as interim chairman of the board of directors. “The Board is committed to ensuring strong leadership to guide XTI Aerospace into its next chapter,” said Ornstein. “We thank Scott for his contributions over the last two and a half years and wish him the best in his next chapter. We are confident that the team, with Jeremy as interim CEO, will serve the best interests of the company and its objectives, employees and shareholders.” “I’m honored to lead XTI at such an exciting inflection point, with U.S. sourcing becoming a critical point of differentiation in the commercial drone market,” said Schneiderman. “Meaningful work lies ahead, and I’m committed to driving disciplined execution and delivering sustained growth. I’m looking forward to continuing to work with the Drone Nerds team as we support our customers in this evolving, high-growth market.” Schneiderman has served as the chief executive officer of Drone Nerds since 2014, and under his leadership, Drone Nerds has grown into one of the premier providers of enterprise drone solutions, services, and hardware in the United States. With more than a decade of experience in the UAV industry, Schneiderman has helped establish Drone Nerds as a trusted authority across multiple sectors through a combination of technical expertise, strong vendor partnerships, and a customer-first approach. He brings a program-focused perspective shaped by supporting organizations as they evaluate, deploy, and scale drone operations through platform selection, training, integration, and long-term support. Ornstein served as chief executive officer of Mesa Air Group, Inc. from 1998 until November 2025 and as chairman of the board of directors of Mesa from 1999 until November 2025. Following his departure, Mesa completed a merger transaction and changed its name to Republic Airways Holdings Inc. Ornstein co-founded Virgin Express S.A./N.V., an airline in Brussels, Belgium, where he served as chief executive officer and chairman from 1995 until 1999. In 1994, Ornstein served as chief executive officer of Continental Express, and was later named senior vice president of airport services for Continental Airlines. Ornstein served as executive vice president and president of Mesa’s then-wholly owned subsidiary WestAir Holding, Inc. from 1988 to 1994. Ornstein began his career in aviation in 1986 with AirLA, a commuter airline in Los Angeles. Mr. Ornstein attended the University of Pennsylvania.
